edges.description: In the one reported case, a narrow upper arch and upper airway accompanied moderate sleep apnea, which CPAP relieved; maxillary expansion over the same period widened the upper arch and airway. The authors attribute the apnea to maxillofacial hypoplasia narrowing the airway, and also propose that the MN1 variant may cause it directly.

edges.description: Shows that Mn1 is required for intramembranous ossification of the cranial skeleton, the developmental process this node says is disturbed.
edges.limitations: The allele removes MN1 rather than producing a stable C-terminally truncated protein, and the dominant phenotype, cleft palate, is rare in the human syndrome. It shows the process depends on MN1, not how the truncated protein disturbs it.

nodes.description: Brain malformations specific to this syndrome include an atypical, focal form of rhombencephalosynapsis with loss of vermis morphology and cerebellar folia crossing the midline, polymicrogyria of the insula extending into the perisylvian region, hypoplastic olfactory bulbs, and a persistent primitive trigeminal artery. MN1 is highly expressed in fetal brain. The cellular steps linking truncated MN1 to these malformations have not been studied.

nodes.description: Midface hypoplasia, skull shape anomalies with occasional craniosynostosis, abnormal posterior clinoid processes and ear anomalies point to disturbed development of the craniofacial skeleton. In mice, Mn1 is required for intramembranous ossification of the cranial vault and for palate closure, but that evidence comes from null alleles rather than from the truncated protein that causes this syndrome.

nodes.description: MN1 contains a large intrinsically disordered region and forms nuclear aggregates that disperse with 1,6-hexanediol and re-form on its removal, behaving as liquid droplet-like condensates. Truncated MN1 forms larger and more intense nuclear aggregates than wild type. A patient-derived frameshift allele also showed nuclear aggregation in transfected cells. Whether altered phase separation contributes to disease is the authors' proposal.

nodes.description: A heterozygous, usually de novo, nonsense or frameshift variant creates a premature stop codon in the terminal exon of MN1 or in the extreme 3' region of exon 1. The founding cohort concluded the disease is caused by a dominantly acting truncated protein and not by haploinsufficiency; a second group termed the variants gain-of-function on the basis of in vitro assays. A dominant-negative contribution was raised by the first group and has not been excluded.
